quiz2.q: The day before yesterday, the “homebody” neuron decided to go for a walk; today it decided to stay in. Nobody retrained it. What changed?
options: The weights: they automatically adjust after every decision made
The activation function: it switched from a threshold to a sigmoid
The inputs: today’s weather and mood are different, while the weights and bias stayed the same
The bias: it builds up day after day, like fatigue
quiz2.explain: The weights and bias are the neuron’s stable “personality”; they change only during training. What changes from day to day are the inputs: the same formula with different x’s gives a different sum and a different decision.

quiz2.q: You want to turn the homebody neuron into a “go-getter” without changing its attitude toward sunshine, rain, and mood. What needs fixing?
options: The bias: make it positive instead of negative
The threshold: raise it higher so the neuron fires more often
The inputs: feed the neuron only good weather
All the weights at once: multiply each one several times over
quiz2.explain: The attitude toward each factor is baked into the weights, while the baseline readiness to act lives in the bias. A positive bias shifts the starting point upward: now even modest arguments “for” are enough to push the sum past the threshold.

quiz2.q: A neuron’s weights: sunshine +0.8, rain −2, mood +0.5. Each input changed by exactly one unit. Which change shifts the weighted sum the most?
options: All three equally: the inputs changed by the same amount, after all
Sunshine: it has a positive weight, and positive influence is always stronger
Mood: internal factors matter more than external ones
Rain: its weight has the largest magnitude, and the sign plays no role here
quiz2.explain: An input’s contribution is the input times the weight, so one unit of change “costs” exactly as much as the weight attached to it. Rain’s weight is −2: in absolute value it beats 0.8 and 0.5, so the sum shifts the most — just downward.

quiz2.q: Predict: how will a neuron behave if all its weights are zero and its bias is −3?
options: It will break: without weights, the neuron can’t compute the sum
It will ignore all inputs: the sum is always −3, and the decision is always the same
It will produce random decisions until it gets trained
It will respond only to the strongest of its inputs
quiz2.explain: Any input multiplied by zero gives zero — nothing of the inputs survives in the sum; only the bias lives there. In any weather whatsoever, such a neuron gives one and the same answer.

quiz2.q: In a network that hunts for cats in photos, a neuron was discovered that fires at the triangle of an ear. Who assigned it that specialization?
options: The programmers: they wrote the rule “a triangle above the head means an ear”
The network’s first layer: it hands out assignments to all the other layers
The data labelers: they traced the ears by hand in the training photographs
Nobody: the specialization emerged on its own when training settled the neuron’s weights into particular values
quiz2.explain: Engineers specify only the architecture: how many layers and how many neurons in each. What exactly each neuron notices is determined by the values of its weights — and those settle on their own during training, which is what the next module is about.

quiz2.q: You copied all the parameters of a trained network — billions of weights and biases — into a new network with exactly the same architecture. What did you get?
options: An exact copy: it will answer the same way, since apart from the architecture and these numbers there is nothing in a network
An empty network: the knowledge stays behind in the original model when you copy
A copy of the “personality” but not the knowledge: learned facts are stored separately from the weights
A blank: it will only start behaving the same after being retrained on the same data
quiz2.explain: A network is fully described by its architecture and parameters: all of its “knowledge” is the values of the weights and biases. Copy the numbers — copy the model; that is exactly why downloading a model means downloading a giant file of numbers.

exercises.q: Explain in your own words how a neuron’s inputs differ from its weights — and why the same weather can lead two neurons with different “personalities” to opposite decisions.
exercises.ref: Inputs describe today’s situation and change from one occasion to the next: sunshine, rain, mood. Weights are the neuron’s stable “personality,” its accumulated experience: they set how strongly, and in which direction, each factor pushes on the decision. The same inputs multiplied by different weights give different sums — which is why the same weather will lure one person outside and keep another at home. It is the weights, not the inputs, that a network tunes during training.

exercises.q: Invent your own real-life “neuron” — any yes/no decision except the walk. Name two or three inputs, give each a signed weight, add a bias, and explain why you chose those particular numbers.
exercises.ref: For example, a “grab coffee on the way” neuron: inputs — tiredness (weight +1.5: the more tired, the more the coffee is needed), the length of the line (weight −1: it pushes away), and minutes until the meeting starts (weight −0.5: being rushed gets in the way). Bias +2: I’m a coffee fiend and inclined to buy by default. Any example works where each factor has a sign (“for” or “against”) and a magnitude (strength of influence), and the bias reflects a baseline inclination before circumstances are even considered.

exercises.q: A friend is convinced: “A language model contains all the texts it was trained on — it just searches them for the answer.” Explain to him what is actually stored inside the model and where its knowledge “lives.”
exercises.ref: Inside the model there are no texts, no database of facts, no rules — only parameters: hundreds of billions of weights and biases, essentially a gigantic table of numbers. Knowledge doesn’t sit in any single cell: it is “smeared” across millions of weights, each nudging the network slightly toward the right answer. That is why downloading a model means downloading a file of numbers, not an archive of texts.
